faq.q: Why is the rim of a pitcher plant so slippery?
faq.a: The rim, called the peristome, has tiny ridges that hold a thin film of water. When it is wet, insect feet cannot grip and they slide in, a bit like a car aquaplaning on a wet road.

faq.q: Why can't insects climb out of a pitcher plant?
faq.a: The walls are coated in loose wax flakes that stick to insect feet and break away. Some pitchers also have downward-pointing hairs or a stringy, sticky fluid.
asks: How does a pitcher plant stop insects escaping?

faq.q: How does a pitcher plant digest its prey?
faq.a: Glands release enzymes into the pool that break down the insect's soft body. Bacteria in the liquid help, and the plant absorbs the nutrients through the pitcher wall.
asks: What is the liquid in a pitcher plant?

faq.q: Why do pitcher plants eat insects?
faq.a: They grow in boggy or rainy places where the soil has little nitrogen. Catching insects gives them the nutrients they cannot get from their roots, while they still make sugar by photosynthesis.

faq.q: Do pitcher plants ever catch bigger animals?
faq.a: Mostly they catch ants and flies, but some large tropical pitchers occasionally trap frogs or small rodents. A few even work with tree shrews, which lick their nectar and leave droppings that feed the plant.
asks: Can a pitcher plant eat a mouse?

facts: Scientists showed in 2004 that the rim of Nepenthes pitcher plants is slippery mainly when it is wet.
Some Bornean pitcher plants, such as Nepenthes lowii, collect droppings from tree shrews that visit to feed on their nectar.
A pitcher is not a flower but a specially shaped leaf.
